findings.why_it_matters: If an attacker has stolen a session cookie (XSS, physical access, synced browser, etc.), the user's standard remediation -- changing their password -- silently fails to evict the attacker's session. Security regression: this diff loosens a control. Session cookies are stateless HMAC signatures over the username, keyed by auth.session_secret, and checked at middleware.py:146 and :198. Rotating the secret was the only revocation mechanism on password change. The reset flow (routes.py:1941) and setup (routes.py:1294) still rotate, so the app now behaves inconsistently: a password reset logs out other devices, but a password change does not.

Side effect of the removal: the acting user's cookie is no longer re-issued. That is harmless now, because the secret is unchanged and the old cookie stays valid. It would matter if rotation were restored without also restoring the re-issue.
Imports: generate_session_secret, sign_session, COOKIE_MAX_AGE and is_secure_request are all still used elsewhere in routes.py (lines 1294, 1329, 1470, 2005), so ruff will not flag them as unused.
No schema or migration impact: the TOML auth.session_secret field is unchanged. No performance impact.

Blast radius: every deployed instance where a user changes their password. Sessions on other devices (including stolen ones) survive the change for up to COOKIE_MAX_AGE. Four existing tests in tests/test_auth_routes.py and tests/test_auth_integration.py will fail.
Verdict: blocking issue, removal of session revocation on password change (impact-1). Revert it, or record an explicit product decision and update the tests.
